message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick‑Reference Overview**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ~99.98 % protium, ~0.02 % deuterium, trace tritium |
| **Physical Properties (gas at STP)** | State | Diatomic gas (H₂) |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (121 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| | Vapor pressure | 1 atm at 20 °C |
| | Specific heat (Cp) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | ~0.9–1.0 near STP |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) |
| | Basic behavior | Forms hydrides (e.g., LiH, NaH) |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Strong H–bond donor/acceptor in H₂O, NH₃, etc. |
| | Reactivity | Highly flammable; reacts with O₂, N₂, metals, halogens under right conditions |
| **Isotopic Differences** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, heavier, used in D₂O (“heavy water”) |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion and radiolabeling |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Tritium half‑life | 12.32 years |
| | Tritium decay energy | 18.6 keV (β⁻) |
| | Deuterium fusion threshold | ~10⁸ K (in stars) |
| **Astrophysical & Cosmological** | Primordial abundance | ~75 % by mass in the Universe |
| | Role in stars | Fusion of H → He powers stars; H‑burning stages (pp chain, CNO cycle) |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| | Solar wind | Dominated by protons (H⁺) |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel | Liquid hydrogen (LH₂) for rockets, fuel cells |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage (metal hydrides, pressurized tanks) |
| | Chemical industry | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Medical imaging | Deuterium MRI, tritium labeling |
| | Electronics | Hydrogen plasma etching, semiconductor doping |
| | Environmental | Clean combustion (water vapor only) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability range | 4–75 % (vol/vol) in air |
| | Explosion limit | 0.02 % (lower) – 0.04 % (upper) for H₂ in air |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause hypoxia by displacing oxygen |
| | Storage pressure | 350–700 bar for LH₂; 200–300 bar for H₂ gas |
| | Cryogenic hazards | Extremely low temperature; requires proper insulation and safety protocols |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Hydrogen is the simplest element** – one proton, one electron, and usually one neutron (protium).  
2. **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but its isotopes give it unique nuclear and chemical properties.  
3. **Its low density and high flammability** make it ideal for rocket propellants and fuel cells, but also require careful handling.  
4. **In stars, hydrogen fusion** is the engine that powers the Sun and other stars, converting mass into energy via the E=mc² relationship.  
5. **Hydrogen bonding** is a key feature in many biological molecules (water, DNA, proteins), influencing structure and function.  

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these categories—whether you’re curious about the quantum mechanics of the H₂ molecule, the engineering of LH₂ tanks, or the role of hydrogen in cosmology!
